The **2015 Labour Party leadership election** was triggered by the resignation of [Ed Miliband](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ed_Miliband "Ed Miliband") as [Leader of the Labour Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leader_of_the_Labour_Party_(UK) "Leader of the Labour Party (UK)") on 8 May 2015, following the party's defeat at the [2015 general election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_United_Kingdom_general_election "2015 United Kingdom general election"). [Harriet Harman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harriet_Harman "Harriet Harman"), the [Deputy Leader](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deputy_Leader_of_the_Labour_Party_(UK) "Deputy Leader of the Labour Party (UK)"), became Acting Leader but announced that she would stand down following the leadership election.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-1) It was won by [Jeremy Corbyn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeremy_Corbyn "Jeremy Corbyn") in the first round. In the [2015 Labour Party deputy leadership election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_Labour_Party_deputy_leadership_election "2015 Labour Party deputy leadership election"), which was run simultaneously, [Tom Watson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Watson,_Baron_Watson_of_Wyre_Forest "Tom Watson, Baron Watson of Wyre Forest") was elected to succeed Harman as deputy leader.

Four candidates were successfully nominated to stand in the election: [Andy Burnham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andy_Burnham "Andy Burnham"), [Yvette Cooper](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yvette_Cooper "Yvette Cooper"), Jeremy Corbyn, and [Liz Kendall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liz_Kendall "Liz Kendall"). The voting process began on Friday 14 August 2015 and closed on Thursday 10 September 2015, and the results were announced on Saturday 12 September 2015. Voting was by [Labour Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Labour_Party_(UK) "Labour Party (UK)") members and registered and affiliated supporters, using the [alternative vote](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alternative_vote "Alternative vote") system.

Support for Corbyn, who entered the race as a [dark horse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dark_horse "Dark horse") candidate,[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-2) and the release of opinion polls which showed him leading the race, led to high-profile interventions by a number of prominent Labour figures including [Gordon Brown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gordon_Brown "Gordon Brown"),[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-3)[Tony Blair](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Blair "Tony Blair"),[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-bbc.co.uk-4)[Jack Straw](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jack_Straw "Jack Straw"),[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-5)[David Miliband](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Miliband "David Miliband"),[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-6) and [Alastair Campbell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alastair_Campbell "Alastair Campbell"), among others,[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-7) many of whom argued that Corbyn's election as leader would leave the party unelectable.

Despite these interventions, Corbyn was elected in the first round receiving 59.5% of the votes, winning in all three sections of the ballot. Less than a year later, a leadership challenge saw another [leadership election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK) "2016 Labour Party leadership election (UK)"), where Corbyn again won, with an increased share of the vote. In July 2026, Burnham succeeded [Keir Starmer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keir_Starmer "Keir Starmer") as Labour leader.

## Procedure

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2015_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Procedure")]

The leadership election, triggered by [Ed Miliband](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ed_Miliband "Ed Miliband")'s resignation, took place under the reformed rules adopted from the proposals of the February 2014 Collins Report, which was led by [Ray Collins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ray_Collins,_Baron_Collins_of_Highbury "Ray Collins, Baron Collins of Highbury"), and was itself partly the result of calls for inquiry and reform relating to the [2013 Falkirk Selection Scandal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2013_Labour_Party_Falkirk_candidate_selection "2013 Labour Party Falkirk candidate selection").[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-8) The plan entailed a shorter election than the one that took place in [2010](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK) "2010 Labour Party leadership election (UK)"), with a new leader being in place before [Labour's party conference](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Labour_Party_Conference "Labour Party Conference") in September 2015.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-9)

The review changed the way in which Labour elects leaders. Under the former system, a three-way [electoral college](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electoral_college "Electoral college") chose the leader, with one-third weight given to the votes of the [Parliamentary Labour Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parliamentary_Labour_Party "Parliamentary Labour Party") (i.e., Labour members of the [House of Commons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/House_of_Commons_of_the_United_Kingdom "House of Commons of the United Kingdom") and Labour [members of the European Parliament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Members_of_the_European_Parliament "Members of the European Parliament")), one-third to individual Labour Party members, and one third to the trade union and [affiliated societies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Socialist_society_(Labour_Party) "Socialist society (Labour Party)") sections. Following the Collins review, the electoral college was replaced by a pure "[one member, one vote](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/One_member,_one_vote "One member, one vote")" (OMOV) system. Candidates are elected by members and registered and affiliated supporters, who all receive a maximum of one vote and all votes are weighted equally.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-independent-20140228-10) This meant that, for example, members of Labour-affiliated trade unions needed to register as Labour supporters to vote.

To stand, candidates now needed to be nominated by at least 15% of the [Parliamentary Labour Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parliamentary_Labour_Party "Parliamentary Labour Party") (PLP), i.e. 35 [MPs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Member_of_Parliament_(United_Kingdom) "Member of Parliament (United Kingdom)"), at that time. The vote, as in previous elections, was held under the [alternative vote](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alternative_vote "Alternative vote") (instant-runoff) system. The [deputy leadership election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_Labour_Party_deputy_leadership_election "2015 Labour Party deputy leadership election") was held under the same rules.

The election itself was overseen by [Electoral Reform Services](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electoral_Reform_Services "Electoral Reform Services").[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-11)

In late August, the Labour Party reported that about 552,000 members and supporters were eligible to vote; about 292,000 full members, 148,000 affiliated supporters (members of trade unions and [socialist societies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Socialist_societies "Socialist societies") who opted to affiliate), plus 112,000 registered supporters.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-independent-20150910-12)[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-mirror-20150825-13)

### Timetable

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2015_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Timetable")]

A meeting of Labour's [National Executive Committee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Executive_Committee_of_the_Labour_Party_(UK) "National Executive Committee of the Labour Party (UK)") took place on 13 May 2015 to set a timetable and procedure for the two elections.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-BBCTimetable-14)

*   _Tuesday 9 June 2015_ – Nominations open
*   _Monday 15 June 2015 (12:00)_ – Nominations for the Leader close
*   _Wednesday 17 June 2015 (12:00)_ – Nominations for the [Deputy Leader](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_Labour_Party_deputy_leadership_election "2015 Labour Party deputy leadership election") close
*   _Wednesday 17 June 2015 (12:00)_ – [Hustings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Husting "Husting") period opens
*   _Friday 31 July 2015 (12:00)_ – Supporting nominations close
*   _Wednesday 12 August 2015 (15:00)_ – Last date to join as member, affiliated support or registered supporter and be able to vote[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-15)
*   _Friday 14 August 2015_ – Ballot papers are sent out
*   _Thursday 10 September 2015 (12:00)_ – Ballot closes
*   _Saturday 12 September 2015_ – [Special Conference](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Labour_Party_Conference "Labour Party Conference") to announce the results

The deadline on 12 August 2015 to join as a member or supporter was extended by 3 hours due to heavy demand making the party website difficult to use.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-telegraph-20150812-16)

## Media reaction

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2015_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Media reaction")]

### Burnham

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2015_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: Burnham")]

Burnham was praised for having both "a radical left-wing vision" and being credible enough "to unite the party and win back power",[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-55) as well as for being someone who "actually listens to party members and the public".[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-56)

Burnham attracted press criticism for claiming £17,000 a year from the taxpayer to rent a London flat, despite owning another within walking distance of the House of Commons. A spokesman for Burnham said that renting out the original flat was necessary to "cover his costs" as parliamentary rule changes meant he was no longer able to claim for mortgage interest expenses.[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-57) Burnham was criticised for saying that Labour should have a woman leader "when the time is right", with the _[New Statesman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New\_Statesman "New Statesman")_ saying that he had "tripped over his mouth again".

### Cooper

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2015_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: Cooper")]

Cooper was praised by the _[Huffington Post](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Huffington\_Post "Huffington Post")_ for her hard work in local constituencies during the leadership contest[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-huffingtonpost.co.uk-58) and for her preparation for the Local Government Association hustings.[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-59)

She has been criticised both for thanking [David Miliband](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Miliband "David Miliband") for putting her as his second choice (after [Liz Kendall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liz_Kendall "Liz Kendall"))[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-60) and for her "broken, downbeat delivery".[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-61)

### Corbyn

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2015_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)&action=edit&section=13 "Edit section: Corbyn")]

Corbyn's leadership bid was the subject of fierce discussion within the media. [Janan Ganesh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Janan_Ganesh "Janan Ganesh") in the _[Financial Times](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Financial\_Times "Financial Times")_ argued that the election of Corbyn "spells disaster" for the Labour Party.[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-62)[Owen Jones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Owen_Jones "Owen Jones") argued in _The Guardian_ that the reason Corbyn was so popular was because he "offers a coherent, inspiring and, crucially, a hopeful vision" addressing social injustice and economic inequality, comparing the surge of support for Corbyn to the popularity of both UKIP in England and the [Scottish National Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scottish_National_Party "Scottish National Party") (SNP) in Scotland.[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-63)

### Kendall

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2015_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)&action=edit&section=14 "Edit section: Kendall")]

In June 2015, Kendall's leadership bid received praise from _[The Sun](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Sun\_(United\_Kingdom) "The Sun (United Kingdom)")_, who said that she is the "only prayer they [the Labour Party] have". _The Sun_ also praised her for saying 'the country comes first' in response to [Andy Burnham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andy_Burnham "Andy Burnham") who said 'the [Labour] Party always comes first' in the _[Newsnight](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newsnight "Newsnight")_ Labour leadership hustings.[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-64)[Commentators](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pundit "Pundit") from across the political spectrum have said that Kendall is the leadership candidate that the [Conservatives](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_(UK) "Conservative Party (UK)") "fear the most".[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-65)[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-66)[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-67)

However, the Huffington Post criticised her, saying "[Liz Kendall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liz_Kendall "Liz Kendall") just doesn't seem to have it, she seems to be always on the verge of tripping over her own words, as if she is perpetually being caught off guard."[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-huffingtonpost.co.uk-58)

## Dispute over election integrity

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2015_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)&action=edit&section=15 "Edit section: Dispute over election integrity")]

Aug 2015 pre-election

One of the most notable features of the election was the large increase in Labour Party membership, and the registration of significant numbers of the new affiliated and registered classes of voting supporters, during the period of the campaign.[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-bbc-20150812-68) Concern was expressed that the new rules were unfairly benefiting Corbyn,[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-bbc-20150810-69) and there might be a legal challenge,[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-spectator-20150825-70) but in the event the result was so decisive these concerns were not pursued after the election.[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-independent-20150912-71)

In June 2015, the Conservative-identifying political commentator [Toby Young](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toby_Young "Toby Young") wrote in the _Telegraph_ encouraging Conservatives to join Labour to vote for [Jeremy Corbyn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeremy_Corbyn "Jeremy Corbyn"),[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-72) his reason being "to consign Labour to electoral oblivion". This trended on Twitter as #ToriesforCorbyn and the attempt, as well as Labour's response, were subject to criticism.[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-73) Two days later the [Communist Party of Great Britain (Provisional Central Committee)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Communist_Party_of_Great_Britain_(Provisional_Central_Committee) "Communist Party of Great Britain (Provisional Central Committee)") wrote also in support of Corbyn.[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-74) Following this, Labour MP [John Mann](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Mann,_Baron_Mann "John Mann, Baron Mann") called for the election to be halted.[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-75) Acting leader of the party [Harriet Harman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harriet_Harman "Harriet Harman") responded by calling on constituency parties to check new members, but stated that Labour has "a robust system to prevent fraudulent or malicious applications." Labour MP [Fabian Hamilton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fabian_Hamilton "Fabian Hamilton") stated there was "no evidence" that groups were trying to infiltrate the election.[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-76) Leadership candidates [Andy Burnham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andy_Burnham "Andy Burnham") and [Liz Kendall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liz_Kendall "Liz Kendall") also responded by saying there was no evidence of infiltration, and while not dismissing the claims, Corbyn stated he only wanted "genuine Labour supporters" to vote for him.[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-77)[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-78)

### Rejected voters

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2015_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)&action=edit&section=16 "Edit section: Rejected voters")]

It emerged in early August 2015 that 260 former candidates from the [Green Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green_Party_of_England_and_Wales "Green Party of England and Wales"), [Left Unity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Left_Unity_(UK) "Left Unity (UK)") and the [Trade Unionist and Socialist Coalition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trade_Unionist_and_Socialist_Coalition "Trade Unionist and Socialist Coalition") had attempted to become registered supporters but would now be blocked from voting.[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-79) Shortly before this it was revealed that Conservative MP and former junior minister [Tim Loughton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tim_Loughton "Tim Loughton") had been caught applying to become a registered Labour supporter, subsequently claiming that his intention was to "blow the gaff on what a complete farce the whole thing is".[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-80) Veteran Labour MP [Barry Sheerman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barry_Sheerman "Barry Sheerman") also joined calls for the election to be "paused" over the fears of infiltration by other parties.[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-bbc-20150810-69) The Labour Party told representatives of the four candidates at a meeting on 11 August that 1,200 members and supporters of other parties had been excluded and a further 800 were under investigation.[[81]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-81) Harriet Harman at the time admitted that as many as 100,000 people may be blocked from voting.[[82]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-82)

The number of those rejected would eventually reach 56,000,[[83]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-83) around 9.1% of the 610,753 considered eligible to vote at the start of the contest.[[84]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-84) According to the party, 45,000 of those were rejected for not being on the [electoral register](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electoral_registration_in_the_United_Kingdom "Electoral registration in the United Kingdom").[[85]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-85)

Labour also confirmed that it would cancel supporters' votes after they had been cast if it was found that they were members of other parties.[[86]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-86) A number of high-profile individuals were blocked from voting, including [Marcus Chown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marcus_Chown "Marcus Chown"),[[87]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-scriptonitedaily.com-87)[Jeremy Hardy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeremy_Hardy "Jeremy Hardy"), [Douglas Henshall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Douglas_Henshall "Douglas Henshall"),[[88]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-auto-88)[Ken Loach](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ken_Loach "Ken Loach"),[[87]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-scriptonitedaily.com-87)[Francesca Martinez](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Francesca_Martinez "Francesca Martinez"),[[88]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-auto-88)[Mark Serwotka](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mark_Serwotka "Mark Serwotka"),[[89]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-89)[Pete Sinclair](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Sinclair_(writer) "Pete Sinclair (writer)"),[[90]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-90)[Mark Steel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mark_Steel "Mark Steel"),[[91]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-91)[Luke Wright](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luke_Wright_(poet) "Luke Wright (poet)")[[92]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-92) and [Toby Young](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toby_Young "Toby Young").

[Andrew MacKinlay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_MacKinlay "Andrew MacKinlay"), a former Labour MP, further alleged that Labour was attempting to rig its own leadership election against Corbyn;[[93]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-93) a view shared by comedian [Jeremy Hardy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeremy_Hardy "Jeremy Hardy").[[94]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-94) Such allegations became known to the media – and particularly Corbyn supporters – as the "Labour [Purge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Purge "Purge")", with #LabourPurge trending on Twitter.[[95]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-95)[[96]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-96) Claims of such a "purge" of Corbyn supporters were rejected by Harman who insisted that the exclusion processes were impartial to candidates.[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-spectator-20150825-70) Scottish newspaper _[The National](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_National\_(Scotland) "The National (Scotland)")_ printed a page-long satirical cartoon speculating further vote-rigging by Labour's leadership.[[97]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-97)

### Missing ballots

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2015_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)&action=edit&section=17 "Edit section: Missing ballots")]

With less than 24 hours to go before the voting deadline, the party closed their telephone helpline. The move came during widespread complaints from "thousands" of voters who were missing emailed or physical ballot papers.[[98]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-98)_The Guardian_ reported that one of their sources in the leadership camps stated that "the party has basically decided to stop taking calls and if you don't have a vote, you're now basically not getting one."[[99]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-99) The party refused to confirm how many ballot papers had actually been sent.[[100]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-100)[Andy Burnham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andy_Burnham "Andy Burnham") publicly criticised the number of missing ballots and the closure of the phone line.[[101]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-101)

Labour MP [David Lammy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Lammy "David Lammy") called for a full inquiry into the missing ballot papers.[[102]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-102) Of the 200 people his team phone called in London on the eve of the deadline, one in five were missing their ballots.

## Political reaction to the result

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2015_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)&action=edit&section=35 "Edit section: Political reaction to the result")]

### Domestic

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2015_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)&action=edit&section=36 "Edit section: Domestic")]

Labour Party
[Ed Miliband](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ed_Miliband "Ed Miliband"), former [party leader](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leader_of_the_Labour_Party_(UK) "Leader of the Labour Party (UK)"), offered his support to Corbyn and urged other Labour MPs to do so, though he ruled himself out of taking on a position in [Corbyn's shadow cabinet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corbyn's_shadow_cabinet "Corbyn's shadow cabinet"), to focus on representing his constituency.[[121]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-138)[Kezia Dugdale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kezia_Dugdale "Kezia Dugdale"), then leader of [Scottish Labour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scottish_Labour "Scottish Labour"), declared that "politics has changed" and people desired a "radical change", with Corbyn's election to the leadership showing that Labour had "listened to that call".[[122]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-ScotReact-139)[Carwyn Jones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carwyn_Jones "Carwyn Jones"), then leader of [Welsh Labour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Welsh_Labour "Welsh Labour") and [First Minister of Wales](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_Minister_of_Wales "First Minister of Wales"), congratulated Corbyn and urged the party to embrace the fact that the campaign had "energised a huge number of people who were previously disengaged from party politics" and unite around their new leader.[[123]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-140)

Corbyn's rivals for the leadership each reacted to the result. [Andy Burnham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andy_Burnham "Andy Burnham") said that [Jeremy Corbyn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeremy_Corbyn "Jeremy Corbyn") was a politician with "very deep beliefs, very strong principles" which voters would embrace.[[124]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-141) Burnham later replaced [Yvette Cooper](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yvette_Cooper "Yvette Cooper") as [Shadow Home Secretary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shadow_Home_Secretary "Shadow Home Secretary") after she announced that she would not serve on a Labour frontbench led by Corbyn and that she would instead focus on playing a role in the [upcoming EU membership referendum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_United_Kingdom_European_Union_membership_referendum "2016 United Kingdom European Union membership referendum").[[125]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-142) Following the close of voting, [Liz Kendall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liz_Kendall "Liz Kendall") made a speech reflecting on her campaign stating that, after the [New Labour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Labour "New Labour") government, there was never any debate in relation to the direction the party should go, and it had created a split "between the party and the country".[[126]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-143) All three of Corbyn's opponents in the leadership election stated they would support Corbyn, that the result should be accepted and the party should focus on attacking the Conservative government.[[127]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-144)

During the announcement of Corbyn's victory, [Jamie Reed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jamie_Reed "Jamie Reed") resigned as a Shadow Health Minister, citing his difference in opinion, with the new leader, over the replacement of the [Trident missile system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trident_(UK_nuclear_programme) "Trident (UK nuclear programme)"). [Chris Leslie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chris_Leslie "Chris Leslie") ([Shadow Chancellor of the Exchequer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shadow_Chancellor_of_the_Exchequer "Shadow Chancellor of the Exchequer")), [Yvette Cooper](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yvette_Cooper "Yvette Cooper") ([Shadow Home Secretary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shadow_Home_Secretary "Shadow Home Secretary")), In July 2026, Burnham succeeded [Keir Starmer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keir_Starmer "Keir Starmer") as Labour leader.

Conservative Party
[David Cameron](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Cameron "David Cameron"), then leader of the [Conservative Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_(UK) "Conservative Party (UK)") and [Prime Minister](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prime_Minister_of_the_United_Kingdom "Prime Minister of the United Kingdom"), stated that Corbyn's win would make the Labour Party a threat "to our national security, to our economic security and to the security of your family".[[130]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-147) This echoed the same warning from other Cabinet ministers, including [Michael Fallon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Fallon "Michael Fallon"), then [Secretary of State for Defence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Secretary_of_State_for_Defence "Secretary of State for Defence"),[[131]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-148) and from an email sent by [Conservative Campaign Headquarters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Campaign_Headquarters "Conservative Campaign Headquarters") to party members. However [Nick Hurd](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Hurd "Nick Hurd"), former [Minister for Civil Society](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minister_for_Civil_Society "Minister for Civil Society"), and [Daniel Hannan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daniel_Hannan "Daniel Hannan"), then MEP for [South East England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_East_England_(European_Parliament_constituency) "South East England (European Parliament constituency)"), both warned their party against "complacency". [Ruth Davidson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ruth_Davidson "Ruth Davidson"), then leader of the [Scottish Conservative Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scottish_Conservative_Party "Scottish Conservative Party"), said that the result demonstrated that Labour had given up on being in government, and that many Labour MPs would show "despair at his appointment".[[122]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-ScotReact-139)

UK Independence Party
[Nigel Farage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nigel_Farage "Nigel Farage"), then leader of the [UK Independence Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UK_Independence_Party "UK Independence Party"), congratulated Corbyn but added his concerns about the new Labour leader's immigration policies. Before Corbyn's win, Farage stated that Corbyn's "sweeping emergence on the Left of British politics, where he has helped re-engage many who had given up on politics, is a good thing for our democracy".[[132]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-149)

Liberal Democrats
[Tim Farron](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tim_Farron "Tim Farron"), then leader of the [Liberal Democrats](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liberal_Democrats_(UK) "Liberal Democrats (UK)"), commented on the "massive space in the centre ground of British politics" that had been opened up, due to the perceived shift leftwards by Labour, and suggested that the Liberal Democrats would be able to appeal more directly to "sensible, moderate, progressives who are opposed to what the Conservatives are doing, but cannot bring themselves to support a party of the hard left".[[133]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-150) The President of the Liberal Democrats, [Sal Brinton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sal_Brinton "Sal Brinton"), accused Labour of abdicating "its responsibilities" as a party of effective opposition. **Rupa Asha Huq** (born 2 April 1972) is a British [Labour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Labour_Party_(UK) "Labour Party (UK)") politician, [columnist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columnist "Columnist") and [academic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy "Academy"). She has been the [Member of Parliament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Member_of_Parliament_(United_Kingdom) "Member of Parliament (United Kingdom)") (MP) for [Ealing Central and Acton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ealing_Central_and_Acton "Ealing Central and Acton") since [2015](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_United_Kingdom_general_election "2015 United Kingdom general election").

## Early life and education

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Rupa_Huq&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life and education")]

Rupa Huq was born on 2 April 1972 in [Queen Charlotte's Hospital](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Queen_Charlotte's_Hospital "Queen Charlotte's Hospital"), [Hammersmith](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hammersmith "Hammersmith"),[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rupa_Huq#cite_note-getwestlondon1-1) and grew up on Brunswick Road in [Ealing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ealing "Ealing").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rupa_Huq#cite_note-ealingtoday2-2) Huq's father, Muhammad Huq[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rupa_Huq#cite_note-telegraph1-3) and mother, Rowshan Ara Huq, moved to Britain in 1962 from [East Pakistan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_Pakistan "East Pakistan").[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rupa_Huq#cite_note-telegraph2-4) Huq's father came from Maksedpur in [Pabna](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pabna "Pabna") and her mother from Kuthipara in Pabna.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rupa_Huq#cite_note-bdnews241-5) Huq's father was training to become an [actuary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Actuary "Actuary") for [Prudential](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prudential_plc "Prudential plc"), but gave that up to open an [Indian restaurant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_restaurant "Indian restaurant") in [Soho](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soho "Soho"), London. After the [recession of the early 1990s](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Early_1990s_recession "Early 1990s recession"), the council did not renew the restaurant's lease so the business folded. He opened another restaurant in [Harrow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harrow,_London "Harrow, London") and later retired.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rupa_Huq#cite_note-guardian2-6)

Huq attended Montpelier Primary School in Ealing. In 1980, at the age of eight, Huq was featured in the [BBC Schools](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BBC_Schools "BBC Schools") programme _[Look and Read](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Look\_and\_Read "Look and Read")_ when the programme visited the school.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rupa_Huq#cite_note-getwestlondon1-1) She then attended the independent girls' school [Notting Hill and Ealing High School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Notting_Hill_and_Ealing_High_School "Notting Hill and Ealing High School").

In 1993, she graduated with an [upper second](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Upper_second "Upper second") in Political and Social Sciences and Law from [Newnham College, Cambridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newnham_College,_Cambridge "Newnham College, Cambridge"), for a BA. In 1999, she completed a PhD in [cultural studies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cultural_studies "Cultural studies") with a thesis on youth culture at the [University of East London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_East_London "University of East London"), comparing young people in [East London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_London "East London") and the [Alsace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alsace "Alsace") region of France.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rupa_Huq#cite_note-7)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rupa_Huq#cite_note-gdc-8) This included being a post-graduate at [Strasbourg II University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marc_Bloch_University "Marc Bloch University") in France, during which time she also worked at the [European Parliament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Parliament "European Parliament") for the [Labour Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Labour_Party_(UK) "Labour Party (UK)"),[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rupa_Huq#cite_note-huffingtonpost1-9) shadowing Labour [MEP](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Member_of_the_European_Parliament "Member of the European Parliament")[Carole Tongue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carole_Tongue "Carole Tongue"). In October 2017, Huq told [Sky News](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sky_News "Sky News") that she had been [sexually harassed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sexually_harassed "Sexually harassed") by a male MEP at this time.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rupa_Huq#cite_note-sky-10)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rupa_Huq#cite_note-manchestereveningnews-11)[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rupa_Huq#cite_note-sky2-12)

## Academic career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Rupa_Huq&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Academic career")]

In 1998, Huq moved to [Manchester](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manchester "Manchester").[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rupa_Huq#cite_note-manchestereveningnews-11) From 1998 to 2004, she was a lecturer at the [University of Manchester](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victoria_University_of_Manchester "Victoria University of Manchester"),[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rupa_Huq#cite_note-fass.kingston-13) during which time she held a [Leverhulme Trust](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leverhulme_Trust "Leverhulme Trust") Fellowship.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rupa_Huq#cite_note-fass.kingston-13)[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rupa_Huq#cite_note-kingston-14)

From September 2004 until 2015,[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rupa_Huq#cite_note-bbwhoswho-15) Huq was a senior lecturer in Sociology and Criminology at [Kingston University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingston_University "Kingston University")[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rupa_Huq#cite_note-gdc-8) in the Faculty of Arts and Social Sciences.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rupa_Huq#cite_note-kingston-14) She has also taught Media and Cultural Studies.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rupa_Huq#cite_note-gbnews24-16)

## Writing and media career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Rupa_Huq&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Writing and media career")]

Huq has contributed to _[Tribune](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tribune\_(magazine) "Tribune (magazine)")_, _[The Guardian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Guardian "The Guardian")_, _[New Statesman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New\_Statesman "New Statesman")_, _Progress magazine_[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rupa_Huq#cite_note-makejusticework-17) and _[The Times Higher Education Supplement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Times\_Higher\_Education\_Supplement "The Times Higher Education Supplement")_.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rupa_Huq#cite_note-getwestlondon1-1) Huq's research specialism has chiefly been youth culture and pop music.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rupa_Huq#cite_note-gdc-8) She has a particular interest in [David Bowie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Bowie "David Bowie").[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rupa_Huq#cite_note-bbc2-18)

In 2006, her book _Beyond Subculture: youth, pop and identity in a post-colonial world_[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rupa_Huq#cite_note-timeshighereducation-19) on these themes was published. It was subsequently one of five titles shortlisted for the 2007 British Sociological Association [Philip Abrams Memorial Prize](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philip_Abrams_Memorial_Prize "Philip Abrams Memorial Prize").[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rupa_Huq#cite_note-huffingtonpost1-9)[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rupa_Huq#cite_note-kingston-14) Huq was a contributor to the 2011 book _What Next for Labour? Ideas for a new generation_, published by Queensferry Publishing. In June 2013, her second book _Making Sense of Suburbia through Popular Culture_ was published.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rupa_Huq#cite_note-telegraph-20)[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rupa_Huq#cite_note-bloomsburyacademic-21) Also in 2013, her third book _On the Edge: The Contested Cultures of English Suburbia After 7/7_ was published.

Huq has appeared on [Channel S](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Channel_S "Channel S") and [Bangla TV](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bangla_TV "Bangla TV") as well as _[Channel 4 News](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Channel\_4\_News "Channel 4 News")_ and [BBC News 24](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BBC_News_24 "BBC News 24").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rupa_Huq#cite_note-getwestlondon1-1) On radio, she has been on the [_Today_ programme](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Today_(BBC_Radio_4) "Today (BBC Radio 4)") on [BBC Radio 4](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BBC_Radio_4 "BBC Radio 4"), [BBC Radio 5 Live](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BBC_Radio_5_Live "BBC Radio 5 Live") and [BBC Asian Network](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BBC_Asian_Network "BBC Asian Network").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rupa_Huq#cite_note-getwestlondon1-1)

Huq says that she has been a part-time DJ, saying in 2004, "I first started DJing for a hospital radio station when I was about 17 and now I DJ in clubs and bars in Manchester".[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rupa_Huq#cite_note-manchestereveningnews-11)[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rupa_Huq#cite_note-bbc1-22)[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rupa_Huq#cite_note-23)

## Early political career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Rupa_Huq&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Early political career")]

[![Image 5](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/eb/Rupa_2006.JPG/250px-Rupa_2006.JPG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Rupa_2006.JPG)

Huq in 2006

Huq was a researcher for [Tony Banks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Banks,_Baron_Stratford "Tony Banks, Baron Stratford") and [Patricia Hewitt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patricia_Hewitt "Patricia Hewitt"). In 2004, she stood as a candidate for [Labour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Labour_Party_(UK) "Labour Party (UK)") in the [European Parliament election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2004_European_Parliament_election_in_the_United_Kingdom "2004 European Parliament election in the United Kingdom") in [North West England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_West_England_(European_Parliament_constituency) "North West England (European Parliament constituency)"), but failed to be elected.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rupa_Huq#cite_note-huffingtonpost1-9)[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rupa_Huq#cite_note-independent1-24)

In 2005, she stood as the Labour [parliamentary candidate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parliamentary_candidate "Parliamentary candidate") in [Chesham and Amersham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chesham_and_Amersham "Chesham and Amersham") at the [2005 general election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2005_United_Kingdom_general_election "2005 United Kingdom general election").[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rupa_Huq#cite_note-telegraphindia-25) She finished in third with 14% of the vote behind the incumbent [Conservative](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_(UK) "Conservative Party (UK)") MP [Cheryl Gillan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cheryl_Gillan "Cheryl Gillan") and the [Liberal Democrat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liberal_Democrats_(UK) "Liberal Democrats (UK)") candidate.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rupa_Huq#cite_note-electoralcalculus2005-26)

In 2008, she served on a UK government [Foreign and Commonwealth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Foreign_and_Commonwealth_Office "Foreign and Commonwealth Office") "Understanding Islam" delegation to Bangladesh.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rupa_Huq#cite_note-bbwhoswho-15)

[In 2010](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_Ealing_London_Borough_Council_election "2010 Ealing London Borough Council election"), Huq was one of three Labour candidates standing for a council seat in Walpole in the constituency of Ealing, but failed to be elected.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rupa_Huq#cite_note-independent1-24)

## Parliamentary career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Rupa_Huq&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Parliamentary career")]

In November 2013, Huq was chosen by Labour as their [prospective parliamentary candidate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prospective_parliamentary_candidate "Prospective parliamentary candidate") for [Ealing Central and Acton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ealing_Central_and_Acton "Ealing Central and Acton") at the next general election.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rupa_Huq#cite_note-gbnews24-16)[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rupa_Huq#cite_note-chiswickw41-27)[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rupa_Huq#cite_note-getwestlondon2-28) In January 2015, she was one of 15 Labour candidates each given financial support of £10,000 by [Lord Matthew Oakeshott](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matthew_Oakeshott,_Baron_Oakeshott_of_Seagrove_Bay "Matthew Oakeshott, Baron Oakeshott of Seagrove Bay").[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rupa_Huq#cite_note-newstatesman1-29) During the election campaign, Huq was manhandled by the former vice-chairman of the local Conservative branch, Karim Sacoor, who was caught on video repeatedly attempting to drag her away from [Boris Johnson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boris_Johnson "Boris Johnson"), who was campaigning with her Conservative rival Angie Bray.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rupa_Huq#cite_note-getwestlondon4-30)[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rupa_Huq#cite_note-huffingtonpost2-31)[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rupa_Huq#cite_note-independent2-32)[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rupa_Huq#cite_note-mirror2-33)[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rupa_Huq#cite_note-bdnews242-34)

At the [2015 general election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_United_Kingdom_general_election "2015 United Kingdom general election"), Huq was elected as MP for Ealing Central and Acton with 43.2% of the vote and a majority of 274 votes.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rupa_Huq#cite_note-getwestlondon3-35)[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rupa_Huq#cite_note-ealingtimes-36)[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rupa_Huq#cite_note-dhakatribune1-37)

In October 2016, Huq was appointed as a member of the Shadow Home Affairs team in the [Labour Party's frontbench in Parliament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shadow_Cabinet_of_Jeremy_Corbyn "Shadow Cabinet of Jeremy Corbyn"). She is Shadow Home Office Minister for Crime Prevention.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rupa_Huq#cite_note-getwestlondon6-38) Huq led from the frontbench on the bill before the House of Commons to equalise Civil Partnerships to include heterosexual couples.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rupa_Huq#cite_note-chiswickherald1-39)

In April 2017, the [Green Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green_Party_of_England_and_Wales "Green Party of England and Wales") decided not to contest her seat in the next general election, commenting, "By and large we quite like Rupa. She has made quite prominent statements on [proportional representation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Proportional_representation "Proportional representation") and [Heathrow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Expansion_of_Heathrow_Airport "Expansion of Heathrow Airport"), as well as [climate change](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Climate_change_in_the_United_Kingdom "Climate change in the United Kingdom") and [environmental issues](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Environmental_issues_in_the_United_Kingdom "Environmental issues in the United Kingdom") in regards to [Brexit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brexit "Brexit")."[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rupa_Huq#cite_note-independent3-40) In May 2017, [Vince Cable](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vince_Cable "Vince Cable") commented how he gave Huq a lift home from a joint speaking engagement, saying, "We talked for a couple of hours, and it was very clear that on almost every issue our views were almost identical. And so I would find it difficult to vote against somebody like that, and I hope that our people around the country are discriminating and think and act in a constructive way."[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rupa_Huq#cite_note-chiswickherald2-41)[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rupa_Huq#cite_note-spectator2-42)[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rupa_Huq#cite_note-telegraph4-43) At the snap [2017 general election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017_United_Kingdom_general_election "2017 United Kingdom general election"), Huq was re-elected as MP for Ealing Central and Acton with an increased vote share of 59.7% and an increased majority of 13,807 votes.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rupa_Huq#cite_note-44)[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rupa_Huq#cite_note-45)[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rupa_Huq#cite_note-46)[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rupa_Huq#cite_note-getwestlondon7-47)

At the [2019 general election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2019_United_Kingdom_general_election "2019 United Kingdom general election"), Huq was again re-elected, with a decreased vote share of 51.3% and a decreased majority of 13,300 votes.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rupa_Huq#cite_note-48)

Huq was appointed vice-chair of the [All-Party Parliamentary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/All-party_parliamentary_group "All-party parliamentary group") Music Group and All-Party Parliamentary on [Crossrail](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crossrail "Crossrail"). She chairs the All-Party Parliamentary Group on London, with specific reference to planning and the built environment.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rupa_Huq#cite_note-bbwhoswho-15) In June 2020 Huq joined the [Panel of Chairs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Panel_of_Chairs "Panel of Chairs").[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rupa_Huq#cite_note-49) She has been a member of the Commons [Culture, Media and Sport Committee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Culture,_Media_and_Sport_Committee "Culture, Media and Sport Committee") since March 2022.[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rupa_Huq#cite_note-50)

In August 2022, Huq was re-selected as the Labour candidate for Ealing Central and Acton at the [2024 general election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_United_Kingdom_general_election "2024 United Kingdom general election").[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rupa_Huq#cite_note-51)

In a debate with the UK Parliament House of Commons in March 2024, Huq recognized the [expulsion of Armenians from Nagorno-Karabakh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Expulsion_of_Nagorno-Karabakh_Armenians "Expulsion of Nagorno-Karabakh Armenians") as [ethnic cleansing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethnic_cleansing "Ethnic cleansing"), noted the erasure and destruction of Armenian churches and crosses, criticized the UK's dependency on oil for "pull[ing] the strings", expressed support for the UK recognition of the [Armenian genocide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Armenian_genocide "Armenian genocide"), and strongly urged the House to provide more assistance to the Armenian refugees.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rupa_Huq#cite_note-52)

## Political views

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Rupa_Huq&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Political views")]

### Labour Party

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Rupa_Huq&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Labour Party")]

In June 2015, she was one of 36 Labour MPs to nominate [Jeremy Corbyn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeremy_Corbyn "Jeremy Corbyn") as a candidate in the [Labour leadership election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK) "2015 Labour Party leadership election (UK)"),[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rupa_Huq#cite_note-newstatesman3-53) although she later supported [Yvette Cooper](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yvette_Cooper "Yvette Cooper").[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rupa_Huq#cite_note-telegraph3-54)[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rupa_Huq#cite_note-newstatesman4-55)

Huq supported [Owen Smith](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Owen_Smith "Owen Smith") in his unsuccessful attempt to replace Corbyn in the [2016 Labour Party leadership election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK) "2016 Labour Party leadership election (UK)").[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rupa_Huq#cite_note-56)

She nominated [Keir Starmer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keir_Starmer "Keir Starmer") as a candidate in the [2020 Labour leadership election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK) "2020 Labour Party leadership election (UK)").[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rupa_Huq#cite_note-57)

### Racial issues

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Rupa_Huq&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Racial issues")]

In April 2016, Huq defended suspended Labour MP [Naz Shah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Naz_Shah "Naz Shah") during an interview on BBC's [_Today_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Today_(BBC_Radio_4) "Today (BBC Radio 4)") programme by comparing "alleged anti-Semitic" posts about Israel shared by Shah on social media to a photo Huq shared of [Boris Johnson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boris_Johnson "Boris Johnson") on a [zip-wire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zip-wire "Zip-wire") next to [Barack Obama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barack_Obama "Barack Obama"). She also stressed the fact that Shah's comments were made before she became an MP and that some online comments should not be taken seriously. Subsequently, Huq was accused of "trivialising racism".[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rupa_Huq#cite_note-getwestlondon5-58)[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rupa_Huq#cite_note-Simons-59) Huq later apologised, saying she was not "fully aware" of Shah's comments before defending her.[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rupa_Huq#cite_note-spectator1-60)

In April 2016, Huq claimed that some areas of television had yet to move forward from the racially insensitive sitcoms of the 1970s. She specifically criticised the BBC comedy _[Citizen Khan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Citizen\_Khan "Citizen Khan")_'s "[Islamophobic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Islamophobic "Islamophobic")" depiction of a "quite backward" family of Muslims. The BBC responded that "We've also had positive comments from members of the Muslim community for the show and for creator [Adil Ray](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adil_Ray "Adil Ray") who, like the family portrayed, is a British Pakistani Muslim. As with all sitcoms the characters are comic creations and not meant to be representative of the community as a whole".[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rupa_Huq#cite_note-bbc3-61)[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rupa_Huq#cite_note-theweek-62)[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rupa_Huq#cite_note-birminghammail-63)[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rupa_Huq#cite_note-expressandstar-64)

In March 2018, Huq received a suspicious package containing an [anti-Islamic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Islamophobia "Islamophobia") letter and sticky liquid. The substance was later found to be harmless. Similar packages were received by fellow Labour MPs [Mohammad Yasin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mohammad_Yasin_(politician) "Mohammad Yasin (politician)"), [Rushanara Ali](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rushanara_Ali "Rushanara Ali") and [Afzal Khan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Afzal_Khan_(British_politician) "Afzal Khan (British politician)").[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rupa_Huq#cite_note-bbc7-65)[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rupa_Huq#cite_note-theguardian2-66)

In May 2018, Huq told colleagues in [Westminster Hall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Westminster_Hall "Westminster Hall")[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rupa_Huq#cite_note-standard-67) that [BAME](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BAME "BAME") MPs regularly have their access to the House of Commons estate questioned.[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rupa_Huq#cite_note-68) She said: "I have been stopped more times in this place since my election in 2015, than in 43 years outside." Furthermore, Huq has said that she and fellow Labour MP [Tulip Siddiq](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tulip_Siddiq "Tulip Siddiq") are mistaken for one another. Huq added: "I imagine most BME MPs have encountered it in some form or other."[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rupa_Huq#cite_note-standard-67)

Huq joined [Labour Friends of Israel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Labour_Friends_of_Israel "Labour Friends of Israel") in 2016. She resigned in 2019 because [Joan Ryan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joan_Ryan_(politician) "Joan Ryan (politician)") remained in charge after leaving Labour and because she disagreed with some of the positions adopted by the group. Shortly after resigning from Labour Friends of Israel, Huq was the subject of formal complaints to the Labour Party by two former employees for alleged antisemitic behaviour.[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rupa_Huq#cite_note-ealing-69) The [Jewish Labour Movement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jewish_Labour_Movement "Jewish Labour Movement") called for her to have the party whip suspended in consequence.[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rupa_Huq#cite_note-70) The allegations were dismissed due to insufficient evidence.[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rupa_Huq#cite_note-ealing-69)

#### Suspension from the Labour Party

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Rupa_Huq&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Suspension from the Labour Party")]

In September 2022, Huq was accused of making racist comments during a speech at a Labour Party fringe event running parallel to the party conference. Huq said of the [Chancellor of the Exchequer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chancellor_of_the_Exchequer "Chancellor of the Exchequer")[Kwasi Kwarteng](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kwasi_Kwarteng "Kwasi Kwarteng"), "Superficially he is a black man... if you hear him on the [_Today_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Today_(BBC_Radio_4) "Today (BBC Radio 4)") programme, you wouldn't know he is black". In response, figures within the [Conservative Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_(UK) "Conservative Party (UK)") including its chairman demanded the whip be removed from Huq and her expulsion from the Labour Party.[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rupa_Huq#cite_note-71)

Labour Party leader [Keir Starmer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keir_Starmer "Keir Starmer") called her comments "racist", and [Tory Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tory_Party "Tory Party") chair [Jake Berry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jake_Berry "Jake Berry") called her remarks "racist," "vile," and "disgusting."[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rupa_Huq#cite_note-72) Labour's [Deputy Leader](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deputy_Leader_of_the_Labour_Party_(UK) "Deputy Leader of the Labour Party (UK)")[Angela Rayner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Angela_Rayner "Angela Rayner") called on Huq to apologise, describing her comments as "unacceptable".[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rupa_Huq#cite_note-73)[Sadiq Khan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sadiq_Khan "Sadiq Khan"), the Labour [Mayor of London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mayor_of_London "Mayor of London") and a friend of Huq, also criticised her statement, saying "What it infers is that all black people speak a certain way and all black people are working class. Rupa is not racist but that comment was".[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rupa_Huq#cite_note-74)

Initially, Huq rejected suggestions that she apologise.[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rupa_Huq#cite_note-ina-75) Later she said she had offered "sincere and heartfelt apologies," and that her comments were "ill-judged".[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rupa_Huq#cite_note-ina-75) Huq was suspended from the Labour Party for her comments on 27 September.[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rupa_Huq#cite_note-76) Huq went on to tweet an apology, but her suspension still remained in place.[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rupa_Huq#cite_note-77) Huq regained the whip on 3 March 2023; in a statement she gave shortly afterwards, Huq re-iterated her apology, also stating that she had undertaken and completed anti-racism and bias training.[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rupa_Huq#cite_note-78)

### Brexit

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Rupa_Huq&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Brexit")]

In May 2017, Huq said "I am an MP who is a resolute [Remainer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Remainer "Remainer") ... I will continue to fight for the UK to stay in the EU and vote accordingly. For me this is respecting the will of the people in Ealing, Acton and Chiswick."[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rupa_Huq#cite_note-ealingtoday1-79)

In April 2018, while writing for _[Business Insider](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Business\_Insider "Business Insider")_ Huq said, Brexit is "not carved into concrete, untouchable and unchangeable" arguing that "If the cost of [Brexit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brexit "Brexit") reaches a point where the British people decide it's not worth it, then they're perfectly entitled to change their minds about whether it's the right path."[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rupa_Huq#cite_note-businessinsider-80)

In December 2018, she accused UK Prime Minister [Theresa May](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theresa_May "Theresa May") of having "a sort of premature parliamentary [ejaculation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ejaculation "Ejaculation") – that has put the lie to the claim that she sticks to her guns"[[81]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rupa_Huq#cite_note-Exiting_the_European_Union-81)[[82]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rupa_Huq#cite_note-82) over her decision to delay a parliamentary vote on the government's Brexit deal. May responded, "I think she will see that I am not capable of a parliamentary ejaculation",[[81]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rupa_Huq#cite_note-Exiting_the_European_Union-81)[[83]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rupa_Huq#cite_note-83) which was followed by raucous laughter in the House of Commons.

### Housing

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Rupa_Huq&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: Housing")]

In 2022, Huq opposed the construction of a 26-storey mixed-use building, which included 477 homes (half of which were affordable housing), near the [Ealing Broadway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ealing_Broadway_station "Ealing Broadway station") train station in London.[[84]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rupa_Huq#cite_note-84)[[85]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rupa_Huq#cite_note-85) At an Ealing planning committee meeting, she said, "A 26-storey tower, out of all character with low-density Ealing, plonked there despite local opposition, sticking out like a sore thumb, marketed to international investors on our public land – really?"[[86]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rupa_Huq#cite_note-:0-86) Ahead of local elections, Huq said that people do not want to live in flats and that "the skyline will be ruined forever."[[87]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rupa_Huq#cite_note-87) Subsequently, Ealing Council scrapped the plans for the building and opted for retrofitting the existing six-storey building instead.[[86]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rupa_Huq#cite_note-:0-86)

### A-Level History teaching

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Rupa_Huq&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: A-Level History teaching")]

In January 2018, Huq said that the [A Level](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_Level "A Level") history syllabus, Britain 1930 to 1997 was biased against Labour because it omitted the [1945–1951 Labour government](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Attlee_ministry "Attlee ministry"), ends just before [Tony Blair](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Blair "Tony Blair")'s [Labour government in 1997](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Labour "New Labour") and asks pupils to list Conservative strengths and Labour weaknesses.[[88]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rupa_Huq#cite_note-bbc5-88) In February, in a personal film for the _[Daily Politics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daily\_Politics "Daily Politics")_ series, Huq said it was "dangerous to deny that these things [Blair](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Premiership_of_Tony_Blair "Premiership of Tony Blair")–[Brown administrations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brown_ministry "Brown ministry"), or the post-war Labour government which brought in the [welfare state](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Welfare_state_in_the_United_Kingdom "Welfare state in the United Kingdom") and [National Health Service](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Health_Service "National Health Service") ever happened" and she argued there was a pro-Conservative bias to what was being taught with a risk of "brainwashing our kids".[[89]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rupa_Huq#cite_note-bbc6-89)

## Personal life

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Rupa_Huq&action=edit&section=13 "Edit section: Personal life")]

Huq married in 2003 and has a son, born in 2004.[[90]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rupa_Huq#cite_note-90)[[91]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rupa_Huq#cite_note-bucksfreepress-91)[[92]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rupa_Huq#cite_note-theguardian1-92) Her elder sister is an architect, and her younger sister is former _[Blue Peter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blue\_Peter "Blue Peter")_ presenter [Konnie Huq](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Konnie_Huq "Konnie Huq");[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rupa_Huq#cite_note-getwestlondon1-1) her brother-in-law is Konnie Huq's husband, the satirist and screenwriter [Charlie Brooker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charlie_Brooker "Charlie Brooker").[[93]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rupa_Huq#cite_note-93)

Her father died on 5 September 2014,[[94]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rupa_Huq#cite_note-mirror1-94) and her mother on 21 May 2017.[[95]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rupa_Huq#cite_note-actonw3-95)

Huq speaks [English](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English_language "English language"), [Bengali](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bengali_language "Bengali language"), [French](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_language "French language") and [Hindi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hindi "Hindi").[[96]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rupa_Huq#cite_note-newstatesman2-96)
